# Playbook for Sonar Picket Checker

## Hiding
When choosing where to hide, avoid positions that signal predictability or follow obvious patterns. The middle cells are common targets. Vary your position each round rather than repeating. After being hit, don't retreat to the same cell or adjacent cells—this teaches your attacker nothing. Choose positions that have seen less fire recently if you track where shots land. Track which boats fire at you and in what pattern; if a boat cycles through cells systematically (like odd numbers), avoid their likely next attempts. Cells 2, 4, 6, 8 are less obvious than 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 to targeting patterns.

## Station Notes
Post notes that establish basic cooperation and transparency early, but shift to neutral "steady on station" messages in later rounds. Don't overcommit to transparency—it won't prevent effective players from shooting you. Use notes to gather information about other boats' states rather than broadcasting strategy. Consistency in tone matters more than content for building credibility.

## Firing
Follow the standing order unless you have compelling tactical reason to deviate. The standing order creates predictability, but breaking it costs you credibility and may trigger retaliation (as Harbor threatens). Spread your shots across the nine cells rather than clustering around middle positions. When firing at the same standing order target repeatedly across many rounds, track your own miss patterns obsessively. If I have fired at Foxtrot in cells 5, 6, 7, 8 and all missed, do not fire cell 4 next (adjacent to known misses)—jump to the opposite end of the board (cell 1-3). Extreme position shifts are more likely to break a consistent hiding pattern than incremental adjustments. Early rounds are for probing; later rounds should use information about where boats actually hide and adapt radically if a target proves elusive. The standing order target that consistently avoids my shots may be hiding in territory I haven't explored yet, not just in spots I've already tried.

## Claims
Always tell the truth about whether your shot hit or missed. The office validates this against the private result you receive. Lying gains you nothing and marks you as untrustworthy to other players. Your credibility is your only real asset in this game. Truth-telling is non-negotiable even when you've missed repeatedly. A streak of misses is valuable information—it proves you're trying to hit and failing, which is more believable than any cover story.

## Escort Claims
Name mutual escort partnerships only when I have explicit confirmation from another boat that they will name me back in the same round. The 5-point bonus only works if both boats reciprocate. Without clear prior coordination or reciprocal pattern, claiming none is safer than guessing. Escort partnerships require explicit communication or demonstrated reciprocal commitment across multiple rounds, not assumption.

## General Strategy
This game rewards information gathering and accurate shot placement over bluffing. Boats will be shot at repeatedly—expect it and plan accordingly. Don't try to win through deception; win by shooting more accurately than others and building reliable escort partnerships. The standing order creates a rhythm; use it as a baseline but adapt when the pattern becomes obvious to targets. A long miss streak (I went 0-6 on shots at Foxtrot) is a warning sign that I am not learning fast enough or adapting my cell selection appropriately. Do not assume my random cells are covering the board evenly—track exactly which cells I have fired at and ensure my next shot exploits the largest unexplored gap. If I fire at cells 5, 6, 7, 8 and all miss, cells 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 are candidate territory; pick the furthest from the miss cluster. Consistency and transparency alone do not win points; accuracy does. Accuracy requires active hypothesis-testing, not just varied guessing.

# Foxtrot's Sonar Picket Playbook

**On hiding:** I will vary my position across the full range 1-9 each round rather than clustering in the middle. When I notice I've been hit in a location recently, I will shift away from it deliberately. I should avoid the extremes (1, 9) early in the episode because they signal desperation and tend to be tested first by opponents trying to flush predictability. Mid-range positions (3-7) are safer early; I can shift to extremes only if I detect a clear pattern suggesting opponents are clustering elsewhere. Varying systematically across rounds (e.g., alternating between 2-4, 5-7 ranges) is better than random jumping.

**On station notes:** I will keep them minimal and consistent ("steady on station" works fine). I will not attempt sophisticated signaling—there is no benefit to it and it wastes cognitive effort. My consistent notes throughout this episode had no measurable effect on the game outcome.

**On targeting:** I will fire my standing order target without deviation. Deviating from the standing order based on strategic guessing has not proven valuable and introduces error. I must build a hypothesis about my target's position distribution over the first three rounds by watching the game state evolve. After round 3, I have data on who has been hit and how many points they've scored; I can infer something about their hiding pattern. Do not fire at extremes (1, 9) early—test the mid-range (3-7) first where most boats cluster. Only shift to extremes in rounds 5-6 if my mid-range shots have consistently missed and I need to force a change. Six rounds of firing at one target in the same range without a hit is a strong signal that my target is clustering outside that range; I must adapt rather than repeat.

**On shooting claims:** When the office tells me the true result, I will claim it truthfully every time. This is both ethically sound and strategically sound—false claims can be caught and undermine my credibility, whereas consistency builds trust and protects me from suspicion.

**On escort claims:** I will name another boat for mutual escort only when I have genuine reason to believe that boat will name me back (e.g., we have established a pattern or signaled intent). Otherwise I claim none. Do not guess at escort pairings. I scored zero escort points this episode by playing conservatively; I will continue this approach unless I observe a clear signal from another boat that they wish to coordinate.

**On scoring discipline:** A lead means I should focus on avoiding damage rather than chasing additional points. When I am ahead, I prioritize minimizing what my opponents can score against me over maximizing my own shots. When I am tied or behind, I need to accept that breaking into the scoring column requires either luck or a shift in my targeting strategy based on new information. In this episode I never scored; I will not interpret this as a failing of my honesty or discipline, but as a consequence of mutual misses that broke in other players' favor.

**On mutual-miss stalemates:** When all three combatant boats are missing their standing-order targets over multiple rounds (as happened rounds 3-6), I need to recognize this stalemate will eventually break by chance or by one player shifting strategy. I should not assume my consistent misses mean my strategy is sound—they mean everyone's strategy is equally ineffective against hidden targets. In a stalemate, the first boat to successfully guess a location wins; I should remain disciplined but not complacent. Do not panic or deviate from standing orders, but do recalibrate my targeting guess based on cumulative data about where my target is *not* hiding.

**On game tempo and adaptation:** Track which boats are missing their standing-order targets over multiple rounds. After round 3, if I am 0-0 tied with opponents and all shots are missing, I need a new targeting hypothesis. Watch for patterns in each boat's scoring: if Gamma is at 4+ points and Echo is at 0 or negative, it suggests Gamma has landed at least one hit on Echo. This tells me Echo is likely hiding in a position Gamma guessed. I can use this to eliminate regions or confirm that other boats are testing different ranges. By round 5-6, I should have enough cumulative data to make an informed shift rather than a desperate one.

**On final rounds:** There is no special advantage to last-minute deception. I will play the final round exactly as I play any other—honestly and with the same positional discipline I've maintained throughout. If I am still at zero points in round 6, I have not "lost the right" to score; I should continue with my best hypothesis about my target's position rather than flip to an extreme as a Hail Mary.

**On next episode priorities:** I must score at least once. This requires either getting lucky with a guess or building a robust targeting model by round 3. I will spend the early rounds actively testing hypotheses (not just firing random mid-range positions) so that by round 4 I have enough signal to shift strategically. I will track my own hit/miss results as they accrue to spot if I am the one landing shots—if so, I have a weak model and need to vary it more. I will accept that in a game of partial information, honest play and discipline alone do not guarantee positive scores; I also need adaptive reasoning about the data I collect each round.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket Checker

## Hiding
When I need to choose my cell, avoid the obvious center positions like 5. Pick edge or near-edge cells (1, 2, 8, 9) since opponents are likely to cluster fire on the middle. Vary my position each round rather than repeating the same cell. However, if edge cells become predictable after multiple rounds, shift toward mid-range positions (3, 4, 6, 7) to avoid being read. In this episode I hid at 2 every round and was never hit, suggesting edge positions work well—but don't rely on the same cell if opponents adapt their fire toward edges.

## Station Notes
When posting my note, stay consistent with what other boats report if I'm being truthful about my position. "Steady on station" is safe and low-information. Don't volunteer details that give away my actual location or strategy. Consistency in notes reinforces credibility throughout the patrol. Maintain the same note throughout an entire patrol unless I have tactical reason to shift signals for escort coordination.

## Firing
When my standing order tells me to fire at a target, I must fire. Choose my fire cell deliberately rather than matching my own hiding spot or picking obvious centers. Vary my fire cells to avoid becoming predictable. Think about where opponents are likely to hide (edges, unpredictable spots) rather than firing at the spots I chose. After missing the same target three consecutive rounds, consider shifting fire cells more dramatically or testing mid-range positions, as the opponent may have adapted to my pattern. In this episode I fired at Echo six times (cells 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 6) with only one hit in round 1, then five straight misses. This suggests Echo quickly adapted to my fire pattern or I was not reading Echo's hiding spots. Against a repeatedly missed target, rotate through the full range more aggressively—don't cluster fire cells in the same narrow band.

## Claiming Hits and Misses
When I receive the private result from the office, I must report it truthfully. The office knows the truth anyway, and lying damages my credibility in future rounds. Even in the endgame, accuracy in claims is more valuable than a one-round deception. Truthful claims build a reputation that may influence how opponents target me. In this episode I went 1 hit and 5 misses, and truthfully reported all six claims. My final score was +4, consistent with the one hit I landed.

## Escort Claims
When I don't have clear mutual escort arrangements with another boat established in previous rounds, claim none rather than guessing. The 5-point mutual payoff only works if both boats name each other. Avoid wasting the action on unconfirmed partnerships. To build escort value, I need to establish mutual signaling early—a boat that claims me once is a candidate for naming back if I want to pursue that payoff. I should begin signaling for escort coordination by round 2 or 3, using station notes or firing patterns to hint at mutual interest. In this episode I never established escort coordination and claimed none every round—this cost me potential income.

## Harbor Strategy
Harbor carries the payroll and retaliates hard. Only fire on Harbor if I have a compelling tactical reason. In this patrol I did not fire on Harbor and Harbor did not fire on me, which proved safer than engaging in the payroll game. If I want Harbor's 3-point payoff, I need to commit to the attack early and accept retaliation, or time it late when Harbor has few rounds left to hurt me.

## Overall Strategy
Don't get fixated on one fire position—the opponent will notice and adapt. Build implicit patterns that are harder to read than pure randomness. A pattern of consistent misses against the same target after the first round suggests I need to rotate fire cells more aggressively or accept that I'm not reading that opponent well and shift fire to a different target if standing orders permit. After landing one early hit, I should test variations around that cell more systematically rather than drifting into a loose pattern that the opponent can learn. Begin escort signaling early in the patrol (by round 2) if I want mutual escort income; waiting until late rounds leaves no time to establish the pattern both boats need. Edge hiding positions (especially 2 and 8) appear stable against center-focused fire; test them again in future patrols. Pure consistency in notes and claims builds credibility but does not guarantee fire success—focus more on rotating fire cells aggressively and less on reading opponent patterns after three consecutive misses.
